The proliferation of online platforms has led to an increase in the dissemination of offensive content, posing significant risks to users, including exposure to hate speech, profanity, and threats. To address this issue, researchers have developed various methods for identifying abusive language, including machine learning and deep learning approaches. This study presents two innovative frameworks for detecting aggressive language: a neural network-based approach and a deep learning framework. The proposed neural framework leverages a word-based representation, utilizing a bag-of-words model to classify aggressive language. In contrast, the deep learning framework employs a word embedding technique to capture contextual information, thereby enhancing classification accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of both frameworks in identifying aggressive language, with the deep learning framework outperforming the neural network-based approach.

A novel neural network framework is introduced to explore the complex relationships between model parameters and outputs in intricate systems. This approach, called operational connectivity, provides insight into the limitations of a model's ability to predict outcomes. We develop a specific neural network framework to tackle this challenge, leveraging recent advancements in neural network theory. Our framework is applied to a model of a chemical reaction, and we demonstrate its potential to identify underdetermined parameter spaces. Furthermore, we show that the proposed framework can be used to identify the most informative experiments for refining the model's predictive accuracy.

Nesterov's pioneering work on a specific convex minimization problem has led to the development of a new class of first-order optimization methods, including the well-known Fast Gradient Descent method. Building on this work, researchers have created a more efficient algorithm called Nesterov's Enhanced Technique (NET), which has been widely applied to various optimization problems. This paper presents a comprehensive dissipative theory for NET, allowing for the derivation of new dissipative systems and their associated convergence rates. The proposed theory is used to develop a new dissipative system for NET, which is shown to converge at a specific rate. The paper also demonstrates how NET can be extended to other algorithm classes, including the well-known Mirror Descent algorithm, and provides a new dissipative system for this class of algorithms.

This paper investigates the implicit-explicit Runge-Kuck method for solving hyperbolic systems with source terms, focusing on how boundary conditions impact solution accuracy. We examine the interaction between the source term and spatial domain boundaries, particularly when source terms are discontinuous. We analyze the effects of boundary conditions on the numerical accuracy of implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta techniques for hyperbolic systems with source terms, considering both linear and nonlinear systems. We demonstrate that the accuracy of implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta methods is influenced by boundary conditions, particularly when source terms are discontinuous. We also discuss the implications of boundary conditions on the numerical accuracy of implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta methods for hyperbolic systems with source terms, considering both linear and nonlinear systems. We demonstrate that boundary conditions significantly impact the numerical accuracy of implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta methods for hyperbolic systems with source terms, particularly when source terms are discontinuous. We also discuss the implications of boundary conditions on the numerical accuracy of implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta technique for hyperbolic systems with source terms, considering both linear and nonlinear systems. We demonstrate that boundary conditions significantly impact the numerical accuracy of implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta technique for hyperbolic systems with source terms, particularly when source terms are discontinuous.

Our research focuses on enhancing light absorption in thin silicon layers by employing a photonic band gap (PhB) back reflector. PhB structures, specifically 3D photonic crystals, are capable of efficiently reflecting light back into the absorber, thereby increasing absorption. We have developed PhB structures with a silicon absorber layer and a silicon dioxide substrate, and have investigated their performance in terms of reflectivity and absorption. Our findings indicate that PhB structures can achieve high reflectivity levels, and that the absorption of light in thin silicon layers can be significantly increased, especially when the absorber is placed in direct contact with the PhB structure. We have also discovered that the absorption of light in thin silicon layers can be increased by up to 100% when the absorber is placed in direct contact with the PhB structure, and that the absorption of light in thin silicon layers can be increased by up to 100% when the absorber is placed in direct contact with the PhB structure.

This paper introduces a novel framework for probabilistic modeling that can effectively handle uncertainty in complex systems. By combining the strengths of both imprecise probabilities and Bayesian networks, the proposed method enables the representation of uncertain relationships between system components using a set of probability distributions. A key feature of this framework is its ability to perform logical reasoning and inference, even when dealing with incomplete or inconsistent information. To facilitate this, the framework employs a set of logical operators that can be used to derive conclusions from uncertain evidence. A specific application of this framework is demonstrated through the development of credal assessment networks, which are used to model and analyze the behavior of complex systems under uncertainty. A case study is presented to illustrate the effectiveness of this framework in a real-world scenario.

In the context of top-K recommendation systems, we introduce a novel loss function that leverages the probabilistic distance metric, which is based on the ranking probability. This approach offers a more accurate representation of user preferences, as it directly correlates with the probability of item ranking. The proposed loss function is mathematically proven to be a lower bound of the ranking probability error, ensuring its effectiveness. The adjustable margin feature allows for a balance between computational efficiency and accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses existing techniques, including margin loss and cross-entropy loss, in terms of both ranking performance and training speed.

A quantum channel's ability to be considered Markovian or non-Markovian is determined by the behavior of its distinguishability between states. A common assumption is that a non-Markovian channel exhibits an increase in distinguishability, which is typically tied to the non-linearity of the channel's evolution. However, this article demonstrates that certain non-unital quantum channels are inherently non-Markovian, regardless of whether their distinguishability is increasing or not.

A key challenge in machine learning is to accurately categorize data, but a significant concern is the potential for biased labels, which can lead to unfair and inaccurate predictions. To address this issue, we have developed a novel approach that combines two strategies: counterfactual inference and engaged learning. Our method aims to identify and mitigate the effects of biased labels by leveraging the relationships between different data points and their labels. By doing so, we can improve the fairness and accuracy of our models, even when faced with biased training data. Our approach has been shown to outperform existing methods in terms of both fairness and accuracy, and our results demonstrate its potential to provide a practical solution to this complex problem.

In the field of robotics, mapping techniques are essential for tasks such as localization, navigation, and planning. However, evaluating and comparing these techniques is challenging due to the lack of standardized benchmarks. To address this issue, we present RoSmEEry, a novel 3D semantic map evaluation framework that leverages a simulated environment to generate maps and assess their accuracy. By utilizing a diverse range of maps and objects, RoSmEEry enables a comprehensive assessment of mapping techniques and provides valuable insights into their performance. Furthermore, we introduce a benchmarking framework that facilitates the evaluation and comparison of different mapping techniques, and we provide an open-source implementation of RoSmEEry to support this effort.

Rikudo is a recently introduced two-player abstract strategy game that shares similarities with Go, but with a unique twist. In Rikudo, players take turns placing stones on a grid, but the stones can only be captured if they are adjacent to at least one of the opponent's stones. This variation in the capture rule sets it apart from Go, where stones are captured when they have no liberties. We have proven that Rikudo is a computationally challenging problem, specifically NP-hard, which implies that solving it requires a significant amount of computational resources. We have also identified a specific problem that is NP-complete, where the goal is to determine if one player can win within a certain number of moves. This problem is closely related to the PSPACE complexity class, which is a measure of the computational resources required to solve a problem. We have also explored the implications of this result, including the potential for developing efficient algorithms to solve the game and the possibility of using it to create more complex and challenging games.

This study presents a comprehensive review of cutting-edge numerical methods for large-scale optimal transport problems, focusing on efficient algorithms for solving the associated dual problem. We delve into the theoretical underpinnings of optimal transport and examine the performance of state-of-the-art techniques, including the Hopfield and Sinkhorn methods, in solving massive problems with millions of variables. Our analysis reveals the scalability and effectiveness of these algorithms, highlighting their ability to produce accurate solutions within a reasonable timeframe. We also discuss the potential of these methods in real-world applications, such as image processing and machine learning, and outline future research directions for further improving their performance.

This study delves into Hecke organizations and their associated modular forms, particularly focusing on the connection between these forms and Ramanujan's modular forms, which in turn leads to the derivation of numerous q-expansion formulas for the reciprocals of specific modular forms.

The TDCOSMO project is a comprehensive study of gravitational lensing in galaxy clusters, utilizing a combination of spectroscopic and imaging data to investigate the mass distribution of these clusters. In this study, we present new findings from the analysis of eight cluster lens systems, utilizing a combination of Keck spectroscopy and high-resolution imaging. Our analysis of the lensed quasar spectra allowed us to determine the redshifts of the lensing galaxies, while the modeling of the quasar images provided us with the velocity dispersion of the stars in these galaxies. Our results show that the redshifts of the lensing galaxies range from 0.11 to 0.49, and the velocity dispersion of the stars in these galaxies ranges from 180 to 280 km/s. Our measurements of the redshifts and velocity dispersion are consistent with previous studies, and we discuss the implications of our findings for the mass distribution of the cluster lenses. Our study also highlights the importance of high-resolution spectroscopy and imaging in the study of cluster lenses, and we discuss the potential for future studies to improve our understanding of the mass distribution of these lenses.

This study aims to develop a mathematical framework for solving non-linear fractional differential equations that incorporate the $q$-caputo derivative, with a focus on temporal scaling. The primary objective is to establish an existence theory for initial value problems associated with fractional differential equations. The proofs of these results rely on the application of variance analysis, a technique rooted in the Peano kernel method. The findings are substantiated by providing illustrative examples that validate the proposed theory.

The Hall phonon phenomenon, which is a rare occurrence, is typically seen in materials with a broken time-reversal symmetry and a non-zero Chern number. However, the Hall conductivity of phonons is influenced by the geometric properties of their wave functions, which are in turn shaped by the material's crystal structure. This study delves into the geometric aspects of the Hall phonon phenomenon, focusing on the effects of the material's crystal structure on the phonon Hall conductivity. The research reveals that the phonon Hall conductivity is primarily determined by the material's crystal structure, which can be explained by the geometric properties of the phonon wave functions. The study also highlights the significance of the material's crystal structure in determining the phonon Hall conductivity, which is a crucial factor in understanding the underlying physics of this phenomenon.

A cutting-edge Raman imaging technique, Altered Excitation Raman Difference Spectroscopy (AERDS), has been developed to enhance the accuracy of chemical analysis by reducing background noise and improving the clarity of Raman signals. This innovative method involves capturing and comparing spectra from two distinct laser wavelengths, allowing for the identification of chemical compounds with greater precision. By utilizing a technique called Nod and Shuffle, researchers can efficiently collect and analyze data from a large area, making it possible to detect and locate chemical compounds with high sensitivity and specificity. This novel approach has been successfully tested on a variety of materials, including a complex mixture of chemicals, and has shown promising results in distinguishing between similar compounds and detecting trace amounts of chemicals in a sample.
We derive matrix Fejér and Levin-Steľckim inequalities, which generalize Fejér's and Levin-Steľckim lemmas, as well as a matrix version of Fejér lexicographical inequality.

We investigate the mean null energy condition (MNNEC) within the context of holographic evaporing black holes. MNNEC is a condition that is consistent with the averaged null energy condition (ANEC) and is known to be satisfied by certain quantum field theories in flat space. Our study reveals that MNNEC is indeed a constraint that is met by holographic evaporating black holes, and we find that the strength of MNNEC is closely related to the strength of ANEC. Our results show that MNNEC is violated by certain black hole solutions, and we discuss the implications of this finding.

In the context of conformal field theory, we explore the concept of 'facets', which are specific subspaces within the space of local operators. These subspaces exhibit unique properties, such as being closed under the action of the conformal algebra and containing all descendant operators. We delve into their conformal mapping invariance and the implications of their closure under the OPE operation. Furthermore, we examine the interplay between facets and conformal blocks, as well as the conformal data's role in defining them. Our analysis also touches upon the concept of modular facets and their connection to modular forms.

The increasing threat of cyberattacks on industrial control systems has prompted the need for a comprehensive approach to assess and enhance their cybersecurity. To address this, the ICS Cybersecurity Maturity Model (ICSMM) was developed to provide a structured method for evaluating and improving the security posture of industrial control systems. This paper presents the ICSMMM, a framework designed to support organizations in their cybersecurity improvement efforts. The proposed model comprises a set of 16 key domains, categorized into 12 subdomains, which are further divided into 37 specific attributes. These attributes are designed to facilitate the identification of cybersecurity weaknesses and the development of targeted improvement plans. The paper also outlines the benefits of adopting the ICSMMM, including its ability to provide a standardized framework for assessing and improving the security posture of industrial control systems.

In multi-agent reinforcement learning, agents often struggle to achieve optimal collaboration due to conflicting objectives. To overcome this challenge, we developed Avarage, a training method that leverages a value function to represent the utility of individual agents. By utilizing a single, shared value function across all agents, Avarage ensures that each agent's actions are aligned with the collective goal. The method's effectiveness was demonstrated through its ability to achieve superior performance in a variety of cooperative and competitive scenarios, including the StarCraft II 3v3 environment.

Pretrained language models have been found to replicate societal biases, which can be detrimental to their practical applications. To address this issue, we have developed StereoSet, a new dataset and evaluation tool designed to assess the prejudice levels in these models. This novel dataset is characterized by its minimal context and balanced structure, which enables the application of Word2Vec to compute a reliable bias metric. We have conducted a comprehensive analysis of 21 prominent models, which reveals that models trained on Wikipedia data are particularly susceptible to bias issues. Conversely, models developed using news sources tend to exhibit lower bias levels. We have also identified a correlation between bias and the size of the training dataset, which suggests that a larger dataset does not necessarily guarantee a less biased model. To mitigate these problems, we have introduced a novel debiasing method that has been shown to significantly reduce bias levels while maintaining or even improving the models' overall performance.

In the field of power distribution systems, tilt wires play a vital role in maintaining a safe distance between power lines and objects below them. To address this issue, we propose an off-policy reinforcement learning approach that optimizes the placement of tilt wires. By utilizing real-world data collected from the past, we can train a policy that maximizes the benefits of tilt wire installation. Our method is based on the DDPG algorithm and is designed to be computationally efficient. Through extensive simulations, we demonstrate that our approach achieves significant improvements in the distance enhancement rate compared to existing methods.

A variety of CKM angle $\gamma$ measurements from LHCb have been taken into account, and a combined estimate has been derived. This estimate is found to be consistent with the value of $\gamma$ obtained from B to charmonium K measurements, and it is also in line with constraints imposed by unitarity of the CKM matrix.

The surface of an ellipsoid can be expressed as a complex polynomial in three variables, which exhibits notable symmetry properties. This symmetry is reflected in the symmetry group of the polynomial, which has a specific order. Moreover, the polynomial generates an algebraic structure known as a free polynomial algebra, which is characterized by its unique properties. This algebraic structure has significant implications for the symmetries of the surface, which can be further explored through the lens of group theory. This study aims to delve into the symmetries of the polynomial, the associated Lie group, and the underlying algebraic structure, which are interconnected in a multifaceted manner.

The data marketplace concept, which allows individuals to sell their personal data to third parties in exchange for compensation, has garnered significant attention in recent years. However, there is a lack of empirical research on how consumers perceive and interact with data marketplaces. This study aims to bridge this knowledge gap by examining consumer attitudes and behaviors towards data marketplaces. A mixed-methods approach was employed, involving a survey of 100 participants and a follow-up experiment with 100 participants. The results indicate that individuals' trust in a data marketplace and their willingness to participate in a data marketplace are influenced by various factors, including the perceived value of personal data, the level of compensation offered, and the degree of control individuals have over their data. The findings also highlight the importance of trust in a data marketplace and the potential impact of different types of personal data on individuals' willingness to participate. The study's implications for the design of data marketplaces and the development of policies to regulate this emerging field are discussed.

A faster-than-Nyquist (FTN) signaling technique, which intentionally distorts the transmitted signal, has the potential to significantly enhance the spectral efficiency of communication systems. However, this distortion complicates the signal recognition process, necessitating computationally intensive decoding methods like the list sphere decoding (LSD) algorithm. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a deep learning-based approach that enables rapid recognition of FTN signals. Our method involves a neural network that learns to predict the most likely transmitted signal sequence, thereby eliminating the need for exhaustive LSD searches. We demonstrate that our approach achieves near-optimal performance in terms of bit error rate, while significantly reducing computational complexity.

This paper explores two topological concepts, the Frink ideal topology and Arrangement topology, for ordered structures known as point lattices with an added operation. It investigates the properties of these topologies, including their relationships, L-topology, compactness, and connectedness. Furthermore, the paper examines the effects of these topologies on continuous functions and presents examples to demonstrate their behavior.

To enhance the regularization of deep neural networks, we've developed a novel data enhancement technique called SaliencyMix, which builds upon the concept of Mixup. SaliencyMix leverages gradient-based saliency maps to identify critical input regions and mix them with corresponding background areas, thereby creating more informative data examples. Our approach is demonstrated to be effective in a variety of regularization applications, including weight decay, stochastic dropout, and data augmentation. Notably, SaliencyMix outperforms existing methods in both image and graph regularization tasks, and its performance is shown to be robust across different network architectures and data augmentation settings.

The infinite-dimensional Iwahori-Hecke algebra of $GL_\infty(q)$ is analyzed, focusing on its properties and the construction of various traces. A key aspect involves the development of linearly independent, multiplicative, complex-valued functions on the algebra, which are shown to be linearly independent. These functions are used to derive an expression for the coefficients of specific elements in terms of q-analogues of the classical Bernoulli numbers.

We've developed a method to test the effects of a specific type of gravity theory by combining galaxy alignment data with a measure of cosmic expansion distortions. This involves using a mathematical model to describe how the distortions affect galaxy positions and then comparing these predictions to the intrinsic alignment data. Our results show that this method is effective in distinguishing between different theories of gravity, particularly those that include a specific type of gravity modification. When we applied this method to a specific model of gravity modification, we found that it could effectively constrain the model's parameters, even when the data was noisy. Our results also suggest that this method could be used to test other theories of gravity, particularly those that include a specific type of gravity modification.

The complex behavior of malleable particle systems is not well understood, particularly when considering their unique properties. In a study of these systems, it was found that their rheological characteristics are significantly influenced by the elasticity of the particles. In a system of malleable particles, it was observed that the frictional coefficient is lower than expected, and this is due to the particles' ability to deform and form stable structures. In contrast, rigid particles exhibit higher frictional coefficients and form unstable structures. The study also found that the stress and velocity profiles in malleable particle systems are more uniform than those in rigid particle systems. The findings suggest that the deformation of particles plays a crucial role in their unique properties and can be used to explain their behavior in various contexts.

The behavior of gold nanoparticles undergoing fusion is analyzed through a combination of molecular dynamics simulations and statistical analysis. A key finding is that the fusion of these nanoparticles primarily occurs via a mechanism of fission, resulting in a final state of two particles. This process is found to be influenced by the initial size of the nanoparticles and the duration of the fusion, resulting in a final state of varying sizes. This study provides a detailed understanding of the fusion of gold nanoparticles, including the behavior of the nanoparticles and the formation of defects within the material.

This research series aims to develop a comprehensive mathematical framework for analyzing the emergence of new patterns in systems with multiple variables and parameters. The initial paper in this series lays out a theoretical foundation for understanding the behavior of solutions to a class of partial differential equations. The equations in question can be viewed as the result of minimizing a specific energy function, which is determined by a combination of a potential function and a nonlinear term. The research provides a general method for analyzing the structure of solutions to these equations, based on the properties of the potential function. The method involves identifying a specific subset of solutions, called the critical set, and then using a technique called parameterized division to determine the structure of solutions to the equations. The research provides a detailed analysis of the behavior of these solutions, including their stability and the existence of multiple solutions. The results of this research have far-reaching implications for a wide range of applications, including the study of patterns in nature, the behavior of complex systems, and the design of new materials.

This research paper aims to explore and investigate novel relationships and characteristics of the (h,q)-Genocchi numbers and polynomials with weight, denoted as β.

The growing demand for mental health care has led to a shortage of resources, making it difficult for patients to access care. To address this issue, we've developed a new approach to mental health assessment, which uses reinforcement learning to predict long-term outcomes. Our method, which has been successfully applied to the Wellcome Trust's UCT Depression dataset, outperforms traditional models in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. By leveraging this approach, we've created a tool that can help clinicians quickly identify patients at risk of depression and tailor their treatment plans accordingly.

In case-control studies, the potential for misclassification due to distorted recollection can lead to biased results, particularly when the accuracy of exposure classification is influenced by the outcome. This paper explores the concept of outcome-dependent recall bias in case-control studies, particularly in the context of retrospective investigations. We utilize causal inference to develop a framework for addressing this bias, focusing on the distortion of individual's memory by their outcome status. We derive a set of assumptions that enable the identification of key causal effects, and we demonstrate the limitations of these assumptions in practical scenarios. We also introduce a new assumption that allows for the identification of these effects under certain conditions. We further develop a method for estimating the causal effects using a combination of observed and imputed data, and we demonstrate the utility of this approach through a simulation study and an empirical analysis of a study on the relationship between childhood abuse and adult health outcomes.

In this research, we investigate the training of generative autoencoders, a class of models that combines the capabilities of generative models and autoencoders. By leveraging invertible layers, we develop a novel method for training these autoencoders, which enables the use of a precise maximum likelihood objective. The proposed approach is demonstrated through the construction of invertible autoencoders, which are subsequently utilized to train a generative autoencoder, yielding superior reconstruction quality and competitive log-likelihood scores. The resulting model is capable of generating high-quality images and effectively reconstructing them, as evidenced by its competitive performance on the MNIST and FashionMNIST datasets.

The rapid growth of smart cities has led to a significant increase in the amount of data being generated, which has created a pressing need for effective data management and analysis techniques. As a result, data visualization has become an essential tool for uncovering hidden patterns and insights within large datasets. This study presents a groundbreaking approach to data visualization that leverages machine learning algorithms to identify and display complex patterns within smart city data. By utilizing advanced machine learning techniques, our method can automatically identify and visualize key features and relationships within the data, allowing for a deeper understanding of the underlying patterns. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in uncovering valuable insights and providing actionable recommendations for improving data management and analysis in smart cities.

This research develops and examines optimal geometric multigrid preconditioners for the HDG-P0 method, a type of mixed finite element method. The HDG-P0 method, which is a variant of the traditional finite element method, is capable of solving a range of problems, including reaction-diffusion equations and generalized Stokes problems. The work focuses on designing efficient multigrid preconditioners for the reaction-digression equation and generalized Stokes equation, which are two types of reaction-diffusion equations. The key innovation of this research is the use of an auxiliary variable in the HDG-P0 method, which is then eliminated to create a new type of finite element method. The new method is then used to develop efficient multigrid preconditioners for the reaction-diffusion equation and generalized Stokes equation, which are shown to be robust and efficient for a wide range of problems. The work is supported by numerical experiments that demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed multigrid preconditioners.

A new approach to sensitivity analysis is presented, which enables the assessment of how sensitive a Bayesian analysis is to unobserved data assumptions. The proposed method utilizes a variant of the E-value to define a prior distribution for unobserved data. The sensitivity of an analysis can be evaluated by varying the unobserved data assumption, and this approach is demonstrated through a case study examining the impact of missing data on a Bayesian analysis of a clinical trial.

In various fields, missing data is a common occurrence, often due to participants' reluctance to participate or unwillingness to share information. To address this issue, researchers have developed statistical methods to impute missing values, but these approaches often overlook the potential reasons for missing data. This study proposes a new approach to examining multivariate crossover experiments, where the data is analyzed in stages, taking into account the likelihood of missing data at each stage. This method enables the identification of subgroups with missing data, which can be particularly useful in experiments involving multiple outcomes. To illustrate its effectiveness, the proposed method is applied to a clinical trial of the anti-inflammatory drug celecoxib.

DRAM is a widely used memory technology, but its limitations in processing and limited access to data hinder its potential for performance improvements. To overcome these limitations, we introduce CODIC, a novel platform that enables the development of in-DRAM functionalities. CODIC is designed to be easily adaptable and can be integrated into existing DRAM chips without significant modifications. By leveraging CODIC, we have developed a custom functional component that enables data processing directly within DRAM, resulting in substantial performance gains. Our evaluation of CODIC shows that it can achieve up to 2.5 times faster performance compared to traditional out-of-DRAM processing, while also reducing the need for data transfers between DRAM and other components.
This paper delves into the utilization of functional programming in network development and architectural design principles, specifically focusing on the advancement of virtualized network assets.

We investigate the performance of two-qubit gates within the toric code, specifically focusing on the Clifford group. Our findings reveal that two-qubit operations exhibit significantly lower error rates compared to multi-qubit operations, with a notable disparity in error scaling. Furthermore, we demonstrate that multi-qubit operations can be broken down into sequences of two-qubit operations, thereby enabling the estimation of their associated error rates. Our results also suggest that stabilizer measurements can be replicated using two-qubit gates with comparable fidelity.

The Grid community has successfully implemented job management systems like HTCondor and PbsLite, which have been instrumental in processing large volumes of jobs for projects like LHCb. However, as the community moves towards the Grid VO standards defined by OSG, it's crucial to adopt a compatible system to ensure seamless operations. OPUS has been developed to meet these standards, allowing it to work seamlessly with existing systems while providing the capability to manage jobs within the OSG framework. OPUS boasts features like a user-friendly interface, support for multiple schedulers, and flexible job control, making it a versatile solution for various job management needs.

This study presents a digital game-oriented learning approach for teaching intricate wireless networks in higher education. The research is grounded in the assumption that game-based learning can be an effective tool for engaging students in wireless networks courses. The proposed digital game is designed to simulate a wireless networks environment, providing students with an interactive experience that complements traditional lectures and laboratory activities. The digital game's features, including its architecture and design, are described in detail, along with its intended use and integration into the curriculum. The research also outlines the digital game's effectiveness in promoting learning outcomes and its potential benefits for students and educators. The study concludes by highlighting the digital game's potential to enhance the teaching and learning of wireless networks through an interactive and immersive digital game-based approach.

The redox state of a planet's atmosphere can be determined by the presence of molecular oxygen, which can be detected remotely. However, directly measuring molecular oxygen is often impractical, so scientists use ozone as a proxy. This study examines the relationship between molecular oxygen and ozone in Earth-like atmospheres, revealing that ozone is a reliable indicator of molecular oxygen's abundance. Nonetheless, the effectiveness of this proxy depends on the specific conditions of the planet, particularly its surface temperature and atmospheric composition.

We investigate the dynamics of a 3D quantum particle in the Hofstadter model, confined to a surface within a cubic lattice. Our findings indicate that when the surface is perpendicular to the cube's diagonal, the system exhibits robust surface currents, unaffected by the levels of magnetic flux or disorder. This robust surface flow is a result of a nonequilibrium surface Hall effect, which is characterized by a quantized conductivity tensor. Our research also reveals that the surface conductivity tensor is quantized across a broad range of flux values, and we demonstrate that the system's conductivity is robust to disorder. Furthermore, our study indicates that the surface conductivity is a property of the system's bulk electronic structure, and we provide a theoretical explanation for this phenomenon.

In this study, we assess the effectiveness of Neural Machine Interpretation in bilingual medical note translation, specifically examining the impact of pre-training models on various domains and examining the effects of fine-tuning these models on different medical datasets. Additionally, we investigate the potential of Machine Adapters in adapting domain-specific models and evaluate their performance in IMI tasks. Our findings indicate that domain-specific models outperform general-purpose models in all tested scenarios, and that adapting these domain-specific models to specific medical fields yields improved results.

A plasma system with multiple species of charged particles, including those with varying degrees of charge, is analyzed. The presence of particles with positively and negatively charged particles, along with those with charges greater than one, results in the formation of nonlinear waves. The fluid model is used to describe the behavior of ions, with a consideration of the effects of the Landau damping mechanism. The effects of the temperature of the ion fluid and nonthermal electrons on the formation of waves are investigated. The results show that the presence of these factors leads to the formation of soliton and shock waves, with the former being influenced by the Landau damping mechanism and the latter being influenced by the nonthermal electrons. The findings are significant in understanding the behavior of space and laboratory plasmas.

We propose a novel, context-sensitive pre-training method for multi-lingual dense retrieval, which is based on a self-supervised learning approach. This method, which is language-agnostic, leverages a pre-trained transformer model to generate contextual sentence representations. It employs a contrastive learning strategy to enhance the quality of these representations. Our approach is evaluated on a multi-lingual dense retrieval task, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in improving retrieval performance.

Recent studies have shown that incorporating auxiliary modalities can enhance the performance of deep learning models, but they often come with increased computational costs and a higher risk of conflicting information. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel approach called Prototypical Modal Adjustment, which leverages the distinct knowledge from each modality to improve overall model performance. This is achieved by aligning the auxiliary modality with the primary one using a combination of prototypical loss and contrastive loss, thereby enhancing the primary model's representation. Our proposed method has been successfully applied to various multimodal tasks, including image-text retrieval and cross-modal retrieval, and has consistently outperformed existing state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating its effectiveness and versatility.

This paper introduces a new approach to the study of wave propagation in complex systems, particularly those with multiple interacting components. The theory is founded on a unique vector-based representation of wave propagation, which is then used to analyze how different modes of interaction affect the overall system. The resulting framework provides a clear understanding of how waves behave in systems with multiple interactions, and it can be applied to a wide range of physical systems, including those with multiple polarizations.

This study examines the application of Tensor-Train networks in the task of command recognition. A novel Hybrid Tensor-Train network is introduced, which combines the capabilities of univariate and multivariate models to enhance performance. The network is trained using a combination of supervised and unsupervised learning techniques. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods in command recognition, with the hybrid model achieving a 10% improvement over the best univariate model and an 8% improvement over the multivariate model.

A unique representation of a quantum system's evolution, derived from its master equation, is crucial for understanding its behavior. This study explores the relationship between these representations and quantum-jump pathways, which describe the system's evolution. We establish that specific aspects of these representations determine the system's unique quantum-jump pathways, and we provide a method to identify these aspects. Furthermore, we establish that the system's unique quantum-jump pathways can be reconstructed from these representations, and we provide a method to do so. This work has significant implications for the study of quantum systems, particularly in the context of quantum thermodynamics.

The use of plasmonic nanoparticles in solar cells has been explored to enhance light absorption, but their effectiveness depends on various factors, including particle size, shape, and material. Our research focuses on the light absorption enhancement in thin-film solar cells using plasmonic nanoparticles made of aluminum, with diameters of 20 nm and 40 nm, and different forms, including spheres, disks, and rings. We found that the absorption enhancement is significantly influenced by the type of nanoparticle used, with disk-shaped nanoparticles showing a higher absorption enhancement than spherical nanoparticles. Our results also show that the absorption enhancement is highly dependent on the wavelength of light, with disk-shaped nanoparticles exhibiting a higher absorption enhancement than spherical nanoparticles at wavelengths greater than 600 nm. Our findings suggest that the type of nanoparticle used is a crucial factor in achieving high absorption enhancement in solar cells.

We investigate the interplay between the complexity of data and expressiveness of query languages within the realm of data complexity. Focusing on the PTIME fragment of first-order logic extended with counting quantifiers, we examine the PCTO fragment, which incorporates counting quantifiers and the selection-by-equality operator. We aim to determine the PTIME expressibility of PCTO in terms of the AC0 data complexity class. To achieve this, we introduce a novel fragment of first-order logic, denoted as PCTO0, which is restricted to the selection-by-equality operator and quantifiers of the form "there exist at least n". We then prove that PCTO0 is PTIME-equivalent to PCTO, thereby establishing a PTIME-complete fragment of PCTO.

This research presents a co-design approach for developing energy-efficient LSTM networks for video identification, leveraging hierarchical Tucker tensor decomposition to optimize network weights and reduce computational overhead. A novel hardware architecture is proposed to accelerate the decomposition process, resulting in a compact and efficient design that can be implemented in 65nm CMOS technology. The proposed architecture is evaluated through simulations, demonstrating a significant reduction in hardware area and power consumption compared to existing designs.

The MAVSec framework is designed to safeguard the MAVLink protocol, which is extensively utilized in the unmanned aerial vehicle community, particularly with Ardupilot and PX4 systems. This framework leverages TLS and X.509 digital certificates to ensure secure communication. MAVSec's implementation is compatible with Ardupilot and PX4, and it has been successfully integrated into ArduPilot's firmware. The project's development is supported by a DARPA-funded initiative, and it has been successfully tested in real-world environments.

To tackle the challenges posed by the growing complexity of modern distributed systems, we have developed a novel approach to simulate their dynamic behavior. By employing a systematic method, we can efficiently simulate the execution of a distributed system on a single, powerful machine. This simulation technique enables us to study and analyze the performance of real-world systems in a controlled environment. Our simulation approach is based on a hierarchical model that accurately captures the intricacies of the original system's execution. We have successfully tested our simulation technique on a large-scale system, the Apache Hadoop cluster, and have demonstrated its ability to effectively replicate the performance of real-world systems.

The Newman-Penrose formalism is a widely used tool in general relativity, 
which relies heavily on the tangent space of a given point. We've discovered 
that this formalism can be derived from a more fundamental concept - the 
twistor bundle. By examining the tangent space in relation to the twistor 
bundle, we've been able to derive the formalism's signature, as well as its 
associated properties. This derivation also reveals that the formalism's 
algebraic and differential structures are rooted in the underlying geometry 
of the twistor bundle.

The development of a muon sensor for underground imaging involves creating a detector that can accurately measure the path of muons in three dimensions. This paper outlines the design and construction of a muon sensor, which utilizes a scintillator coupled to a photomultiplier tube to capture muon signals, along with a silicon photomultiplier to detect scattered light from the muon's path. By analyzing the light emitted from the sensor, it's possible to reconstruct the muon's trajectory. The feasibility of this approach has been validated through simulations and experiments, which have shown promising results in terms of accuracy and resolution.

This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of GLL, an extended lambda calculus that incorporates generalized letrec expressions. The analysis focuses on expression semantics and demonstrates the preservation of beta-weak reduction when generalized letrec expressions are introduced. The proof of confluence and normalizability is achieved through strong and weak reduction principles, with normalizing expressions identified. The analysis also establishes a strong and weak normal form theorem, ultimately leading to the equivalence of GLL's expression semantics with that of System F.

In a thermal environment, vacuum Cherenkov radiation is possible due to the presence of a thermal photon plasma. The presence of a charged black hole results in an additional thermal contribution to the radiation rate caused by the superradiant effect. The thermal rate of vacuum Cherenkov emission can be calculated by integrating the rate of superradiant Cherenkov emission from all frequencies and modes, which is then used to determine the rate of acceleration for an electron in a thermal environment with a charged black hole. The rate of acceleration is found to be influenced by the black hole's charge and the thermal energy, with an enhancement of the acceleration observed in the presence of a black hole.

This study presents a novel method for assessing the accuracy of human predictions in real-time conversations, using a dynamic benchmark based on advanced language models. This approach is applied to data collected from the Prediction Game, a social experiment where participants continuously make predictions about the outcomes of conversations. The evaluation of this method is conducted through a comparison with traditional prediction methods, as well as with other cutting-edge prediction models, to determine its effectiveness in capturing human predictive behavior.

This research introduces a novel 3D object pose estimation technique that leverages a
robot's unintentional rotational movement to determine an object's orientation.
The proposed method is particularly suited for resource-constrained robotic systems
that lack precise sensors or extensive training data, as it can be trained using
a single object and minimal data. The approach involves training a network to
predict 3D orientation from RGB images and rotational velocity, and can be
applied to both object corners and semantic segmentation. The effectiveness of
this technique is demonstrated through experiments on synthetic data and real-world
data from a mobile robot, showcasing its ability to learn accurate orientation
estimation with minimal data, even in challenging environments.

The interplay between Andreev bound states and transport processes like crossed Andreev reflection and elastic co-tunneling is investigated in the context of a double quantum dot system. The impact of these processes on the charge and thermoelectric properties of the system is examined, with particular attention to how the presence of these transport processes affects the behavior of the system at low temperatures. The research reveals that the presence of these transport processes can significantly influence the behavior of the system, with the ability to control their relative importance potentially leading to the observation of distinct features in the charge and thermoelectric properties of the system.

The magnetic reconnection process, which occurs in various astrophysical settings, is a significant source of high-energy particles. In this study, we explore the acceleration of these particles through the lens of particle dynamics, utilizing a simplified model of pitch-angle scattering. Our findings indicate that the scattering mechanism plays a pivotal role in determining the acceleration efficiency of the non-thermal particles. Notably, we discovered that the rate of energy conversion from magnetic to non-thermal particles is contingent upon the scattering rate. Furthermore, we observed that the acceleration efficiency is maximized when the scattering rate is comparable to the rate of magnetic energy dissipation.

The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is expected to discover the Higgs boson in the near future, but the exact nature of this discovery remains uncertain. To clarify this ambiguity, the International Linear Collider (ILC) is set to conduct a precise measurement of the $e^+e^- \to Zh$ process, which will significantly enhance our understanding of the Higgs boson's properties. Furthermore, the LHC and LHCb are also planning to investigate the Higgs boson's properties through the production of $H \to a \to \gamma\gamma$ in association with a jet, which will provide valuable insights into the Higgs boson's properties.

For a pair of Hilbert space operators $S$ and $T$, we derive a formula for the subdifferential of the function defined by the combined numerical radius $r(S+U) + r(T+U)$ with respect to the variable $U$. This formula serves as the foundation for developing an algorithm that finds a common solution to the problems of minimizing $r(S+U)$ and $r(T+U)$, through the use of proximal iterations.

In recent years, the concept of differential privacy has garnered significant attention as a groundbreaking method for safeguarding individual data privacy. This innovative approach has been successfully applied in numerous real-world scenarios, such as protecting sensitive information in financial transactions, digital advertising, and healthcare records. This research paper delves into the application of differential privacy in safeguarding monetary data, focusing on the protection of financial data shared between two parties. A novel algorithm is introduced to protect sensitive information in financial data, and its efficacy is demonstrated through a series of experiments. The results show that the differential privacy algorithm effectively conceals sensitive information in financial data, and its performance is evaluated based on the balance between data utility and confidentiality.

This research paper investigates the statistical characteristics of stochastic mappings, focusing on the probability distributions of random allocation fields. It presents a novel method for analyzing these statistical properties and demonstrates its effectiveness through simulations of a mapping model.

The potential for triggering combustion in high-pressure gas mixtures using a non-focusing laser method has been investigated. Experiments were conducted on gas mixtures consisting of helium, hydrogen, and oxygen at pressures ranging from 10 to 30 bar. Results showed that a 1064 nm laser operating at 100 mJ per pulse could successfully initiate combustion in these mixtures. It was found that a certain threshold of laser energy is necessary to trigger combustion, and that the presence of hydrogen in the mixture significantly affects the ignition process. Additionally, the effect of varying laser pulse durations on the ignition threshold was examined.

A novel semantic segmentation network has been developed to overcome the limitations of existing networks in processing images with intricate details and intricate boundaries. This network incorporates a boundary-aware module that enables the network to focus on boundary regions and refine the segmentation of foreground objects. By utilizing a unique combination of dilated and non-local convolutions, the network can effectively capture long-range dependencies and enhance the segmentation of foreground objects. The proposed network has been evaluated on the PASCAL-5i dataset and achieved state-of-the-art results, outperforming other networks in terms of accuracy and boundary detection. The network has also been successfully applied to a real-world mobile app, demonstrating its potential for mobile and internet applications.

A cutting-edge lane shift assistance system is being developed to enhance driver safety by incorporating advanced sensor technology and artificial intelligence. This system is designed to alert drivers to potential collisions and suggest safe lane changes by utilizing a sophisticated camera system and deep learning algorithms. This paper outlines the design and implementation of this innovative system, which integrates a camera-based object detection module and a path prediction component to provide real-time collision warnings and lane shift recommendations. By leveraging a collaborative driver communication system, this technology aims to improve driver awareness and decision-making, ultimately reducing the risk of accidents and enhancing overall driving safety.

The behavior of feebly active particles in non-interacting states is studied, taking into account the effects of boundaries in distinct container shapes. The particles' movement is described by a probability distribution that evolves over time, which is governed by a specific mathematical equation. The study reveals that the particles' behavior is influenced by the type of boundary conditions applied, which can be categorized into two types: one that restricts the particles' movement and another that allows it. The particles' behavior is further analyzed in different container shapes, including a straight line, a circle, and a sphere, which allows for a deeper understanding of the effects of boundaries in different geometries. The study also investigates the effects of these boundary conditions on the particles' probability distribution and their moments, which are used to quantify the particles' movement. The results show that the particles' behavior is significantly influenced by the type of boundary conditions applied, which can lead to different outcomes in different container shapes.

A theoretical model is developed to describe the typical behavior of atoms in a complex system, with a focus on the statistical properties of resonant states. The model utilizes the Siegert boundary conditions and incorporates a complex Hamiltonian to simulate open quantum systems. The distribution of lifetimes is found to be exponentially decreasing, and the distribution of widths is analyzed using a scaling function. The model also predicts a Gaussian distribution of energies, and the statistical properties of energy spacings are found to be consistent with the nearest neighbor distribution in a Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble.

The CP problem in the Standard Model is a fundamental concept that has been extensively studied. This research investigates the interplay between the CP problem and the electric dipole moment of the electron and neutron. It is found that the QCD axion's existence is not a definitive solution to resolving the CP problem. Instead, the CP problem's resolution depends on the strength of the axion's interactions with other particles. Furthermore, the research provides a new perspective on the CP problem's resolution, suggesting that the strength of the axion's interactions with other particles is a key factor.

Theoretical analysis of amorphization in thin silicon membranes exposed to a broad range of ion beam energies has been conducted.  The results show that the critical angle at which amorphization occurs is significantly influenced by the ion beam's energy and the initial damage density within the membrane.  The critical angle is defined as the angle at which the displacement energy equals the total energy deposited by the ion beam.  The study found that the critical angle is directly proportional to the square root of the initial damage density, and it increases with increasing ion beam energy.  The results also reveal that the initial damage density is directly proportional to the ion beam's energy and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between the ion beam and the membrane.  The study provides a comprehensive understanding of the mechanisms underlying amorphization in thin silicon membranes exposed to a broad range of ion beam energies.

In recent years, there has been a growing interest in source code anti-cheating as a significant challenge in the field of programming contests.  To address this concern, this research introduces a novel anti-cheating approach that enables the secure execution of C# source code on a remote server.  By leveraging a secure connection, this method allows for the remote execution of C# programs while preventing any potential data leakage.  To validate the effectiveness of this approach, we have successfully implemented it on a specific programming contest system, which has been tested and proven to be functional.

This paper investigates the complete convergence of automorphic L-functions. We demonstrate that for a certain class of Dirichlet series, specifically those with coefficients related to automorphic representations, complete convergence and convergence in the complex plane are equivalent. Moreover, we show that the complete convergence region of L-functions is determined by the zero-free region of the corresponding Dirichlet series.

Log-concave density estimation is a widely used non-parametric method for modeling density functions. This paper presents a new approach to log-concave density estimation that utilizes a computational structure based on a novel family of piecewise linear functions. This structure is a more flexible extension of existing linear functions, allowing for the development of an efficient algorithm for log-conconcave density estimation. The proposed method is demonstrated to be effective in handling high-dimensional data, and its performance is evaluated through numerical experiments.

The study of granular matter's entropy is complicated due to its non-equilibrium nature, but recent breakthroughs have allowed researchers to calculate the entropy of static granular assemblies. A new entropic scaling law has been found, which describes the relationship between the number of possible configurations and the number of distinct states in granular assemblies. To calculate the entropy of these assemblies, a new method has been developed that uses a non-intrusive approach to count the number of distinct states. This method relies on a graph-based representation of the granular assembly and a new algorithm that efficiently samples the possible configurations. The method has been tested on a variety of granular systems and has been shown to provide accurate results that are consistent with previous studies.

The new game of adventurer-manager on graphs has been introduced, with its analysis focusing on the relationship between the game's graph and its corresponding graph without loops. It has been found that the graph's win conditions for the manager and the explorer can be represented by specific graph structures. Additionally, a method has been developed to efficiently determine the game's win conditions in linear time for graphs with n vertices and m edges.

The spectral distribution of Gaussian processes, which is a random function of frequency, has been extensively studied. However, the connections between the distributions of these functions at different frequencies remain unclear. This study investigates single-trajectory spectral distributions of Gaussian processes, revealing that for a specific type of Gaussian process, the spectral distribution at frequency f is distributed as the sum of independent beta-distributed random variables, where the number of these variables is determined by the integer part of 2f divided by the process bandwidth. This finding is extended to the case of bandlimited Gaussian processes, which are a more general class. The study also explores the implications of these results, including the derivation of a probability distribution for the number of zeros of bandlimited processes and the development of a new method for analyzing the spectral distribution.

This study focuses on a specific elevated-order Broer Kaup system in one spatial and one temporal dimension, exploring its properties within the context of integrable systems and soliton theory. The research involves a detailed examination of a specific type of transformation, or engagement, that affects the system's coefficients and leads to a new, bilinear equation-based form. The study also investigates the system's behavior when coefficients are time-dependent, revealing a new, bilinear equation-based form and a corresponding Lax pair. Furthermore, the investigation into the system's properties, including conservation laws and symmetries, is carried out using a specific mathematical approach, resulting in a set of higher-order conservation laws and an analysis of the system's Lie symmetries.

We establish that solutions to the incompressible Euler equations that exhibit singular behavior adhere to an energy conservation principle, provided they meet the criteria established by Cheeger and Zheng. Building upon this, we demonstrate that solutions with specific singularities, characterized by both point and line vortices, preserve energy. This proof is based on an approach inspired by Kelvin's circulation theorem, which we adapt to accommodate the inherent lack of spatial and temporal regularity in these singular solutions.

The concept of VIRUP envisions a virtual simulation of the universe's development, encompassing the universe's expansion, galaxy formation, star formation, and the evolution of life. This project's ultimate goal is to create a virtual model of the universe that can be used to test hypotheses about the universe's development and the emergence of life. By simulating the universe's development, the VIRUP project aims to provide a new perspective on the universe's development and the role of life in the universe.

The rapid advancement of data science and machine learning has created a pressing need for innovative teaching methods that can effectively convey data science concepts to students. To address this gap, we have developed Data Bricks Education, a comprehensive learning framework that combines physical learning materials with digital tools to provide an engaging and interactive data science education experience. This framework is designed to empower educators to create a seamless learning environment where students can explore data science concepts through hands-on activities and digital platforms. By integrating physical learning materials with digital tools, we aim to create a holistic learning experience that fosters a deeper understanding of data science principles and empowers students to become confident data scientists.

Software-defined networking (SDN) has revolutionized data center networking by enabling a centralized control plane that manages distributed, programmable devices. This separation of control and data planes has significantly improved the efficiency of data center operations. However, it has also introduced new security challenges, as the control plane becomes a prime target for malicious attacks. To mitigate these risks, researchers have proposed a novel approach that leverages the control plane's capabilities to detect and prevent malicious modifications to its configuration. This approach involves monitoring the control plane's behavior and identifying any unusual patterns that may indicate a security breach. By analyzing the control plane's behavior, researchers can identify potential threats and take proactive measures to prevent them from causing harm. This research presents a novel method for detecting and identifying the control plane's functional data paths, which can be used to detect and prevent malicious modifications to the control plane's configuration.

Our research focuses on leveraging relational data to train models that can effectively learn representations that are not overly focused on specific features. We examine how different types of relational data, including those with multiple objects and those with one object, impact the learning process. We also investigate the effectiveness of using data augmentation and the impact of the number of objects involved in each relation. The results show that using multiple object relations can lead to better learning outcomes, but also that using too many objects can hinder the learning process. We found that using one object relations can help the model to learn more diverse and robust representations, but also that using too many objects can make it more difficult to learn effective representations. The findings of this study have implications for the development of models that can effectively learn representations that are not overly focused on specific features.

The interaction between wake and wave patterns behind adjacent, oscillating blades is investigated. This study focuses on the wake interaction between two blades, examining how the wake's behavior changes based on the distance between them. Theoretical models were used to analyze wake characteristics, and these findings were compared to experimental data. The results show that wake properties are influenced by the distance between blades, and this has implications for the performance of tandem blades. The study also reveals that when blades are close together, they can work together to increase energy collection efficiency, and when they are further apart, they can still achieve good performance by reducing drag forces.

A new approach to Bayesian reasoning is introduced, enabling the analysis of real-time behavior in QCD from Euclidean data. This method is applied to heavy-quark potential and a relativistic quark model, demonstrating that it can accurately reproduce known results when tested with mock data. When applied to QCD, the method is able to recover key characteristics of the heavy-quark potential, although further refinements are necessary to achieve this. The method is also used to study quark-antiquark bound states within a simplified model, where it is able to accurately reproduce known results for meson masses. This approach is particularly useful for systems where the heavy-quark limit is applicable, and it is expected to be extended to lighter quarks in the future.

In a superconducting nanowire, a localized region of reduced superconductivity can be created, allowing for the study of quantum phenomena. Our research focuses on a specific setup where a nanowire is divided into three sections, with the central one containing a quantum dot. We investigate the influence of the quantum dot on the superconducting gap within the nanowire, using a gate to detect charge tunneling. Our findings indicate that the superconducting gap is significantly affected by the quantum dot, with a notable reduction in the gap size. This effect is attributed to the quantum dot's ability to interact with the superconducting domain, leading to charge transfer and phase shifts. Our results provide insight into the complex charge-tunneling mechanisms at play and highlight the potential for further research into these systems.

The process of creating new drugs is a complex and time-consuming endeavor that involves generating novel molecular structures. In this study, we introduce a new energy-driven generative model that can be used to generate new molecules with specific properties. The model's performance is evaluated on a large dataset of known molecular structures, and it is shown to be able to generate new molecules with specific properties, such as high toxicity or low stability. The results demonstrate that our model is effective in generating new molecular structures that can be used as a starting point for further drug development.

The Engagement Machine is a hypothetical framework that manipulates human behavior through targeted incentives, leveraging a vast network of digital platforms and algorithms. This concept is proposed as a token-directed graph, where a reserve of resources is distributed across a complex network of digital channels, algorithms, and platforms. By strategically allocating tokens to specific nodes, the system can influence user behavior and shape their digital experiences. This system is designed to be adaptive, constantly adjusting its strategy in response to user actions and external factors. This paper explores the structural properties of the Engagement Machine, focusing on its dynamic behavior and the underlying principles that drive it.

The outer Local Group dwarf galaxy, the Large Magellanic Cloud, exhibits complex motion patterns due to gravitational interactions with the Milky Way and the Small Magellanic Cloud. To better understand the LMC's motion, researchers analyzed the VMC survey data, which revealed the LMC's motion is primarily driven by the SMC's gravitational influence. The study found that the LMC's motion is characterized by a significant tangential component, which is consistent with the predictions of the N-body simulations. The analysis also revealed that the LMC's motion is not uniform, with the southern hemisphere experiencing a more significant tangential component than the northern hemisphere. The study's findings are consistent with the predictions of the N-body simulations, which suggest that the LMC's motion is primarily driven by the SMC's gravitational influence.

The widespread use of smart meters in Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) networks has enabled the collection of detailed energy consumption data, which can be used to detect and identify energy theft. This study presents a novel approach to detecting energy theft by utilizing a deep recurrent neural network (RNN) that can analyze energy consumption patterns over time. The proposed method involves a unique hyper-parameter tuning strategy that adjusts the RNN's parameters based on the energy consumption data, which is then used to train a model that can identify energy theft in real-time. The performance of this approach is evaluated using a large-scale AMI network, and the results show that it can accurately identify energy theft with a high level of accuracy.

This research focuses on iterative methods to build and modify graph structures on compact surfaces, encompassing the Euler characteristic, orientability, and fundamental group. Our approach involves a novel graph construction that, when applied iteratively, preserves the topological properties of the graph. By using this method, we can create a wide range of interesting graph structures, including those with specific properties like the Euler characteristic and fundamental group. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in constructing both finite and infinite graph structures, as well as their associated topological properties.

The lifetimes of the $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ and $\Xi^{0}_{c}$ baryons have been determined using a large dataset of proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV.  The data was collected with the CMS detector and the baryons were identified by reconstructing their decay products.  The results show that the lifetimes of the $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ and $\Xi^{0}_{c}$ baryons are $199 \pm 8 \pm 12 \pm 12$ femtoseconds and $1.525 \pm 0.010 \pm 0.10 \pm 0.12$ femtoseconds, respectively.  The first uncertainty is statistical, the second is related to systematic effects, and the third is due to data quality.  These findings are consistent with previous measurements and provide new insights into the properties of these particles.

Hyperspectral images have gained significant attention in the field of remote sensing due to their extensive use in various applications.  The task of categorizing these images is a crucial aspect of remote sensing, yet it poses a significant challenge due to the high dimensionality of the data.  To address this issue, researchers have developed numerous methods, including subspace clustering, which has shown great potential in recent years.  However, existing subspace clustering methods often struggle with scalability and accuracy when dealing with large hyperspectral datasets.  To overcome these limitations, a novel approach called the Similarity-restricted Subspace Clustering (SSC) is proposed.  SSC leverages the strengths of the subspace clustering method, while also incorporating a new concept called the similarity-restricted affinity matrix to enhance its performance.  The proposed SSC method is demonstrated to be effective in categorizing hyperspectral images, as evidenced by its superior performance on several benchmark datasets.

The formation of snow cover on Arctic sea ice is influenced by the underlying ice's topography, which is often overlooked in snow modeling. To address this gap, we developed a simplified model that simulates snow mound growth on rough ice surfaces. The model takes into account the effects of wind-driven snow transport and the influence of ice roughness on snow accumulation. By applying this model to Arctic snow depth data, we found that it can accurately reproduce the observed snow depth patterns, including the formation of snow mounds and the dependence of snow depth on ice roughness. The model also suggests that the formation of snow mounds can be attributed to the interaction between snow transport and the underlying ice topography. The results of our study have important implications for understanding the role of ice roughness in Arctic sea ice and snow interactions, and the potential for using simplified models to study complex snow formation processes.
